examples.text: He had no speech prepared, so he improvised.

She improvised a lovely solo.

Chiefly in on the mend: improvement in health; recovery from illness.

examples.text: Though he was fearfully weak, he found himself actually feeling better. The disease had spent itself, and the mend had begun.

glosses: Recompense; restoration or reparation, especially (Christianity) from sin.

examples.text: My trousers have a big rip in them and need mending.
When your car breaks down, you can take it to the garage to have it mended.

examples.text: He mended the fire and turned the meat on the greenwood racks.

examples.text: Her stutter was mended by a speech therapist.

examples.text: Cudgell thy braines no more about it, for your dull aſſe vvill not mend his pace vvith beating, […]

glosses: To correct or put right the defects, errors, or faults of (something); to amend, to emend, to fix.

examples.text: Salt Earth and bitter are not fit to ſovv, / Nor vvill be tam'd or mended vvith the Plough.

examples.text: Yee may sir, (quoth he), mend three nayes with one yee.

glosses: To restore (someone or something) to a healthy state; to cure, to heal.

examples.text: Yearly thy Herds in vigour vvill impair; / Recruit and mend 'em vvith thy Yearly care: […]

examples.text: VVill you goe vvith me, vvee'll mend our dinner here?

glosses: To repair the clothes of (someone).

examples.text: "Ready?" said the old gentleman inquiringly, when his guests had been washed, mended, brushed, and brandied.

glosses: To cause (a person or animal) to gain weight; to fatten.

glosses: To advance to a better state; to become less bad or faulty; to improve.

examples.text: Then would ye mend as the fletcher mends his bolt, / Or sowre ale mendeth in summer, […]

glosses: Followed by of: to recover from a bad state; to get better, to grow out of.

To advantage, to avail, to help.
